title: Classes, fields, and inheritance
keyIdeas: `new` creates an instance and `constructor` initialises it.
`#private` fields are only reachable inside the class body.
`extends` + `super(...)` build on a parent class; call `super` before `this`.
Classes are not hoisted: declare before use.

workedExample.problem: Build a `Stack` and a subclass `BoundedStack(capacity)` whose `push` throws a `RangeError` once `capacity` items are stored. Keep the item storage private.
steps: Store items in a private field `#items` in the base class and expose `push`, `pop`, and a `size` getter.
In `BoundedStack`, the constructor must call `super()` before setting `this.capacity`.
Override `push`: check `this.size` against the capacity, then delegate to `super.push(value)`.
Confirm the private field cannot be read from outside the class.
workedExample.answer: Pushing a third item into `new BoundedStack(2)` throws `RangeError`; after one `pop()` (which returns `"b"`) the size is `1`, and `#items` stays hidden.

pitfalls: Using `this` in a subclass constructor before calling `super()`, which throws a `ReferenceError`.
Calling a class without `new` (`Stack()`), which throws a `TypeError`.
Defining state in the module scope instead of on the instance, so every instance shares it.

citations.quote: Classes are a template for creating objects. They encapsulate data with code to work on that data.
The constructor method is a special method for creating and initializing an object created with a class.
It's an error to reference private fields from outside of the class; they can only be read or written within the class body.
Private fields can only be declared up-front in a field declaration.
If there is a constructor present in the subclass, it needs to first call super() before using this.
unlike function declarations, class declarations have the same temporal dead zone restrictions as let or const and behave as if they are not hoisted.
